title: The Four Pillars: Defining Success at the Start of the Year (and Often Thereafter) https://davestuartjr.com/the-four-pillars-defining-success-at-the-start-of-the-year-and-often-thereafter
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart presents the Four Pillars of High School Success, a framework he and three colleagues developed for ninth-grade transition work, as a concrete answer to his broader strategy of defining success wisely, early, and often. He diagnoses the motivational problem this solves: many students hold either a murky, undefined notion of success or an overly narrow one reduced to all As, and both versions make it hard to access sustained motivation. The four pillars, academic success, social success, a plan for the future, and enjoying the process, were originally defined with explicit, measurable benchmarks so that success felt achievable regardless of a student's starting point or ability level. He notes that he's loosened the explicit definitions over time but still teaches and reinforces the four pillars relentlessly throughout the year through mini-sermons, reflection questions, and closing routines, treating repetition as essential to the strategy's effectiveness.
points: The Four Pillars framework was deliberately designed so success is accessible to every student regardless of academic preparedness or ability, not just high achievers.

Stuart's original benchmarks (a GPA floor, one club or activity, a rough-draft postsecondary plan, self-care habits) show how he operationalized an abstract value, success, into concrete, checkable behaviors for ninth graders.
He treats repetition, not a single opening-week lesson, as the active ingredient, reinforcing the four pillars all year through mini-sermons, warm-up questions, and closing routines.
quotes: For most students, success is a deeply ambiguous and murky thing. And for many others, success is an overly simplistic thing, like all As.
In both kinds of student heart, those with no clear definition of success and those with grade-focused ones, accessing motivation for learning is very difficult.

How could we teach ninth graders to think of success as something each of them could access, each of them could value, and each of them could keep working towards no matter their preparedness or ability?

Plan for the future: a clearly stated articulation of the student's current, rough-draft plan for high school and beyond. Enjoy the process: laughter, learning to work efficiently so you have more time for fun, and practicing good self-care habits.
I do teach them at the start of the year and reinforce them relentlessly via things like mini-sermons, warm-up reflection questions, and the occasional end-of-lesson circle.
Do take seriously the need to define success for your students, wisely, early, and often.
